crawler.headline: AI crawler documentation expanded IP ranges, standardized UA strings, and formalized page-level opt-outs across major vendors.
crawler.body: Over the past year, AI crawler documentation has undergone significant standardization and transparency expansion. Major vendors—OpenAI, Amazon, Google, and Anthropic—published or updated consolidated crawler pages with explicit user-agent strings, IP ranges, and opt-out mechanisms, moving away from scattered or ambiguous guidance. A key shift is the emergence of page-level opt-outs (e.g., Amazon's `noarchive` meta tag, Cloudflare's canonical redirects for AI training crawlers) alongside traditional robots.txt directives, giving site operators more granular control. IP-range publication, once absent or incomplete (notably Anthropic's prior "we do not publish ranges" stance), is now standard practice, enabling firewall-level bot verification. The ecosystem also absorbed emerging conventions like `llms.txt` machine-readable site indexes and AI-specific robots.txt directives, with Cloudflare and others building visibility and control tooling around them. Simultaneously, documentation URLs and JSON endpoints underwent structural changes—notably Google's renaming of `googlebot.json` to `common-crawlers.json`—requiring tool and infrastructure updates from operators relying on static endpoint references.

ecosystem.headline: Agentic AI traffic reshapes content infrastructure as publishers and regulators fight for control
ecosystem.body: The last 30 days reveal two intersecting pressures reshaping the AI content ecosystem. On the infrastructure side, agentic AI traffic has exploded—DataDome reported a 50x surge in Model Context Protocol (MCP) usage as Anthropic expanded connectors, forcing platforms like DataDome and Cloudflare to purpose-build triage and trust controls. Publishers, meanwhile, are escalating legal and technical action: the News Media Alliance filed amicus briefs against scrapers like Perplexity, demanded Common Crawl restrictions, and coordinated with tools like Cloudflare Redirects and Arc XP to enforce training-data access rules. Regulators moved in parallel, with the EU simplifying AI rules while banning nudification tech and the UK CMA intensifying algorithm scrutiny. The net effect: content access is fragmenting into negotiated channels (licensing deals), technical gates (virtual waiting rooms, bot detection), and legal boundaries—signaling that the era of open scraping is over and the era of infrastructure-mediated AI content flows has begun.

agent.headline: Infrastructure maturation and bot-identity standards move from theory to production deployment.
agent.body: The past month marks a inflection point: OpenAI and infrastructure partners have transitioned agent systems from experimental to production-grade, while industry consensus on identity and authentication standards has crystallized. OpenAI's sequence of releases—Windows Sandbox implementation, security frameworks, workspace agents in ChatGPT, and voice integration—signals confidence in autonomous agent deployment at scale. Simultaneously, IETF's publication of the Agent Identity, Trust, and Lifecycle Protocol (AITLP) and Cloudflare's shift toward behavior-based detection over binary bot/human framing indicate the ecosystem is settling on common authentication and verification layers. Sea Limited's engineering deployment of Codex agents and expansions into WebSocket optimization suggest adoption is accelerating beyond proof-of-concept. The tension between rapid capability expansion and formal standardization appears resolved: standards are enabling, not blocking, production readiness.
